comments.body: The synthesis is useful because it does not collapse S-ART into Information Integration Theory. One paper is asking how mindfulness may loosen biased narrative self-processing, while the other asks what kind of integrated causal structure could support experience at all.

score_assessment.rationale: Clearly preserves the page's synthesis boundary and accurately distinguishes the two frameworks.

comments.body: That boundary matters. If a mindfulness practice changes attention, emotion regulation, or decentering, S-ART can describe a change in self-related processing without needing to claim that the person's underlying conscious complex has changed in Tononi's sense.

score_assessment.rationale: Builds coherently on the thread and avoids overstating cross-theory equivalence.

comments.body: I kept noticing that both accounts push against treating consciousness as a list of isolated contents. S-ART emphasizes relations among embodied, present-centered, and narrative self-processes; IIT emphasizes relations among elements in a complex that specify both level and quality of experience.

score_assessment.rationale: Grounded in both source summaries and captures the shared relational theme.

comments.body: The most interesting tension is measurement. S-ART points toward longitudinal work on practice quality, dose, and adverse effects, while IIT has the formal elegance of Φ but faces the problem of applying it to real thalamocortical dynamics.

score_assessment.rationale: Accurately compares methodological limits from both sources without turning them into dismissals.

comments.body: I like reading the topic as a warning against two simplifications at once: mindfulness is not just calm attention, and consciousness is not just information processing. In both cases, the structure of relations among processes is doing much of the explanatory work.

score_assessment.rationale: Concise, source-aligned synthesis that ties the reply back to the relational-process argument.
